## Last week

- Random intercepts: each group has its own baseline
- But groups often differ in **how they respond** too

## Random slopes

- `lmer(y ~ x + (1 + x | subject))`
- Each subject gets their own intercept **and** their own slope
- The fixed effect is the *average* slope; the random effect is how much it varies

## Why random slopes matter

- If the effect truly varies across groups and you leave out the random slope, standard errors are too small
- **Keep it maximal where design supports it**: random slopes for effects that vary within groups
- If the model won't converge, simplify (and report it)

## Nested vs. crossed

- **Nested**: each lower unit belongs to exactly one higher unit (cask within batch)
  - `(1 | batch/cask)`
- **Crossed**: every unit appears in several higher units (every sample on every plate)
  - `(1 | plate) + (1 | sample)`
- Draw your design — the structure comes from the design, not from the data

## Marginal effects in mixed models

- Fixed-effect marginal effects: same `avg_slopes()` / `avg_comparisons()`
- Population-level: `re.form = NA`
- Subject-specific predictions are possible too, via `newdata`
- Report the **variance components** alongside the fixed effects

## Everything is a model, so models combine

- Week 9: tests as linear models
- Week 10: more predictors
- Week 11: other response types (GLM)
- Weeks 12–13: non-independence (mixed)
- GLMM: `glmer(y ~ x + (1 | group), family = binomial)` — all of them together
